papers.title: Bayesian model updating via streamlined Bayesian active learning cubature
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel Bayesian active learning method for Bayesian model updating, which is termed as "Streamlined Bayesian Active Learning Cubature" (SBALC). The core idea is to approximate the log-likelihood function using Gaussian process (GP) regression in a streamlined Bayesian active learning way. Rather than generating many samples from the posterior GP, we only use its mean and variance function to form the model evidence estimator, stopping criterion, and learning function. Specifically, the estimation of model evidence is first treated as a Bayesian cubature problem, with a GP prior assigned over the log-likelihood function. Second, a plug-in estimator for model evidence is proposed based on the posterior mean function of the GP. Third, an upper bound on the expected absolute error between the posterior model evidence and its plug-in estimator is derived. Building on this result, a novel stopping criterion and learning function are proposed using only the posterior mean and standard deviation functions of the GP. Finally, we can obtain the model evidence based on the posterior mean function of the log-likelihood function in conjunction with Monte Carlo simulation, as well as the samples for the posterior distribution of model parameters as a by-product. Four numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method compared to several existing approaches. The results show that the method can significantly reduce the number of model evaluations and the computational time without compromising accuracy.

papers.title: ORDINAL-EVIDENTIAL DYNAMIC HYPERGRAPH STATE-SPACE LEARNING FOR RELIABLE CHILD ENGAGEMENT RISK PREDICTION
papers.abstract: The recognition of children's engagement and behavioural risk is critical to building a trusted AI-based approach to education and mental health support. However, current work shows that common engagement-recognition methods lack modelling of complex facial–temporal interactions, do not capture the ordering of engagement states, are prone to class imbalance, and often yield overconfident predictions in ambiguous behavioural settings. This study introduces OE-DHSSNet and the ER-MOBH optimisation strategy for uncertainty-aware and explainable engagement assessment. A selective state-space temporal encoder models long-range behavioural dependencies at low computational cost, and the framework establishes dynamic hypergraph relationships among behaviour-related, facial, and motion cues. An ordinal-evidential prediction head jointly estimates engagement levels and predictive uncertainty, while ER-MOBH jointly optimises predictive performance, calibration, and inference latency under constraints. The framework is built around the DAiSEE dataset, which provides four-level engagement labels, and also includes an EmotiW-based branch for out-of-distribution reliability analysis. In an illustrative, simulation-based evaluation designed to exercise the intended experimental protocol, the optimised OE-DHSSNet configuration reached an accuracy of 95.81%, a macro-F1 score of 94.45%, and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.947, with an expected calibration error of 0.023 and an expected latency of approximately 32.6 ms per video sample. Explainability analysis further indicated that, for the 'Very High' engagement category, the eye/upper-face contribution (44%) was higher than for the 'Very Low' engagement condition (19%), whereas the head-pose/motion contribution was lower for 'Very High' (14%) than for 'Very Low' (42%). Evidential uncertainty correspondingly grew from 0.06 to 0.24, the expected direction for increasingly ambiguous behaviour. The proposed framework can thus help future educational-monitoring and early behavioural-risk-support AI systems, which must be trustworthy, by offering a unified approach to ordinal engagement recognition, uncertainty quantification and calibration, multi-objective optimisation, and interpretable behavioural assessment.
papers.venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences

papers.title: Beyond Xerostomia: A Two-Year Follow-Up Case Report of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Health in Primary Sjögren Syndrome
papers.abstract: Primary Sjögren syndrome (pSS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by chronic salivary gland dysfunction that predisposes patients to oral complications and tooth loss.Although dental implant therapy has demonstrated favorable survival rates in patients with pSS, evidence regarding long-term peri-implant soft tissue health remains limited.This report describes the diagnosis of pSS following implant rehabilitation and highlights the impact of the disease on peri-implant health during a two-year follow-up.A 61-year-old man underwent implant placement at sites 14 and 16 with simultaneous sinus floor elevation and connective tissue grafting.Several months later, he developed progressive xerostomia, xerophthalmia, burning mouth symptoms, and dysphagia.Histopathological examination of a minor labial salivary gland biopsy revealed focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (Chisholm and Mason grade 3), with findings considered compatible with Sjögren syndrome in the clinical context.Following rheumatologic management with hydroxychloroquine and pilocarpine, the patient was monitored for two years.Clinical examination demonstrated persistent xerostomia and generalized gingival and peri-implant mucosal inflammation, whereas radiographic evaluation showed stable peri-implant bone levels without marginal bone loss.This case supports current evidence indicating that implant osseointegration and short-term survival can be maintained in patients with pSS despite chronic hyposalivation.However, it also illustrates that persistent salivary dysfunction and immune dysregulation may predispose peri-implant tissues to mucosal inflammation in the absence of radiographic bone loss, emphasizing that peri-implant tissue health should be evaluated independently of implant survival.Dental implants appear to represent a reliable rehabilitation option for patients with pSS when combined with individualized supportive care.Nevertheless, long-term success should be assessed not only by implant survival and marginal bone stability but also by careful monitoring of peri-implant soft tissue health.Early recognition of Sjögren syndrome by dental practitioners and multidisciplinary management are essential for optimizing both systemic and implant-related outcomes.

papers.title: STATIC VERSUS DYNAMIC NAVIGATION PREDICTABILITY AND THE EMERGENCE OF SMART, BIOSENSOR-INTEGRATED IMPLANTS IN MODERN IMPLANT DENTISTRY: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
papers.abstract: Digital technologies have transformed implant dentistry over the past two decades, with static computer-assisted implant surgery (sCAIS) and dynamic computer-assisted implant surgery (dCAIS) now established as predictable means of transferring a virtual implant plan to the surgical field. This narrative review synthesises current evidence on the comparative predictability of sCAIS and dCAIS, with particular attention to unresolved questions of cost-effectiveness, learning-curve burden, and performance in immediate post-extraction and severely atrophic sites, before examining the parallel but far less mature field of smart, biosensor-functionalised implants. A structured search of PubMed, ScienceDirect and related databases identified systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomised and retrospective clinical studies, and narrative reviews published predominantly within the last decade. Both sCAIS and dCAIS achieve clinically acceptable accuracy, with meta-analytic entry-point deviations in the region of 1.0-1.4 mm and angular deviations of approximately 3-4 degrees, and neither modality shows consistent, clinically decisive superiority over the other. Dynamic navigation appears to preserve this accuracy in immediate extraction sockets and in severely resorbed ridges, including transcrestal sinus procedures, although this evidence base remains comparatively small. Cost, equipment footprint, and a steep operator learning curve continue to constrain the routine adoption of both workflows, and robust economic analyses are lacking. Sensor-functionalised implants capable of monitoring micromotion, pH, and peri-implant inflammation remain overwhelmingly confined to bench-top and early translational studies, held back by miniaturisation, powering, biofouling, and an immature regulatory pathway. Both fields require standardised outcome reporting, prospective economic evaluation, and, for smart implants, dedicated regulatory frameworks before they can be considered routine clinical tools.
papers.venue: Global journal of research in medicine and dentistry

papers.title: PERI-IMPLANTITIS PHENOTYPING AND MANAGEMENT: DIAGNOSTIC HETEROGENEITY AND THE EVIDENCE GAP IN IMPLANT SURFACE DECONTAMINATION AND RE-OSSEOINTEGRATION
papers.abstract: Peri-implantitis is now recognised as the principal biological complication underlying late dental implant failure, yet the field continues to lack a single, universally applied case definition. Divergent probing-depth thresholds, inconsistent baseline reference points for marginal bone loss, and variable inclusion criteria across studies have produced prevalence estimates ranging from single digits to almost half of all implants surveyed, complicating both epidemiological comparison and clinical decision-making. Compounding this diagnostic heterogeneity is a second, related uncertainty: no decontamination protocol for the exposed implant surface has yet demonstrated clear superiority, and predictable re-establishment of true osseointegration (re-osseointegration) after treatment remains the exception rather than the rule. This narrative review synthesises the contemporary literature on peri-implantitis case definitions and clinical phenotyping, appraises the comparative evidence for mechanical, chemical, air-abrasive, laser-assisted, and electrolytic decontamination protocols, and evaluates surgical (resective and reconstructive) treatment outcomes with specific attention to histological and radiographic evidence of re-osseointegration. A structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for the period 2008–2026, prioritising World Workshop consensus reports, systematic reviews with meta-analysis, and randomised controlled trials. The findings confirm that diagnostic thresholds remain probe- and defect-morphology-dependent rather than universally fixed, that defect configuration is the dominant determinant of treatment selection, and that decontamination method choice appears less influential on clinical outcome than completeness of debridement, defect containment, and adherence to structured supportive peri-implant care. Emerging electrolytic and combined chemo-mechanical protocols show early histological evidence of re-osseointegration in humans, but the evidence base remains limited to small cohorts. Standardised, validated phenotyping frameworks and adequately powered trials with re-osseointegration as a histological endpoint are identified as priorities for future research.
papers.venue: Global journal of research in medicine and dentistry

papers.title: Engineering Spatially Localized Bioactive Microenvironments in Assembly Implants for Spatially Extended Bone Ingrowth
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The repair of large segmental bone defects requires implants that combine structural stabilization with biological regulation. Here, we developed a bioadaptive modular implant integrating porous titanium (Ti) alloy for structural reinforcement with spatially localized β‐tricalcium phosphate (β‐TCP) modules for bioactive regulation. Using a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA)‐based diffusion‐confined model, we identified spatial differences in β‐TCP‐associated calcium distribution and corresponding position‐dependent changes in hBMSC proliferation, adhesion, osteogenic differentiation, and Wnt/β‐catenin‐related signaling. The proximal region showing the strongest biological responses was used as a model‐derived spatial reference for organizing β‐TCP‐containing modules. In a rabbit femoral segmental defect model, the Ti alloy/β‐TCP assembly implant showed greater bone formation and ingrowth than porous Ti alloy controls. Histology further revealed that newly formed bone was preferentially associated with β‐TCP‐containing regions and extended into adjacent porous Ti structures. These findings demonstrate a proof‐of‐concept for translating experimentally characterized spatial biological responses into the spatial organization of structural and bioactive implant components.

papers.title: LONG-TERM PERFORMANCE OF METAL-FREE ALTERNATIVES IN IMPLANT DENTISTRY: A CRITICAL REVIEW OF ZIRCONIA AND MODIFIED POLYETHERETHERKETONE (PEEK) IMPLANTS COMPARED WITH GRADE 4/5 TITANIUM
papers.abstract: Titanium (grade 4 commercially pure and grade 5 Ti-6Al-4V) alloys remain the benchmark fixture materials in implant dentistry on the strength of several decades of cohort and randomised evidence. Growing esthetic demand, concern over thin soft-tissue biotypes, and interest in metal-free rehabilitation have driven adoption of yttria-stabilised tetragonal zirconia polycrystal (Y-TZP) implants and, more recently, modified polyetheretherketone (PEEK) as alternative fixture and abutment materials. This review critically appraises the published evidence on the long-term (>10 year) clinical performance, fatigue strength and survival of zirconia and PEEK implants relative to grade 4/5 titanium. A narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and mechanical fatigue studies indexed in MEDLINE, Cochrane CENTRAL and Embase was undertaken. Zirconia implants demonstrate cumulative survival rates approaching those of titanium at 5-7 years (94-98%) and a pooled 10-year cumulative survival rate near 95%, together with consistently favourable pink-esthetic and soft-tissue outcomes, but fracture-driven failure, particularly of narrow-diameter one-piece designs, remains a distinguishing mechanical weakness. Direct RCT evidence comparing zirconia with titanium is limited to two to four trials with follow-up rarely exceeding 5-7 years. PEEK implants and PEEK-based abutments offer a low elastic modulus that reduces stress-shielding but show fatigue limits and fracture toughness inferior to titanium under ISO 14801 testing, and clinical fixture-level survival data beyond the short term are essentially absent. No RCT was identified that directly compares fatigue strength and long-term survival of zirconia or PEEK against grade 4/5 titanium implants over a 10-year horizon. Titanium therefore remains the material of choice for load-bearing and long-span indications, while zirconia is a reasonable metal-free option in esthetically demanding, lower-load sites pending longer-term randomised data; PEEK's clinical role remains provisional and adjunctive rather than as a definitive fixture material.
papers.venue: Global journal of research in medicine and dentistry

papers.title: Physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (PIKANs) for noise-robust reconstruction of boiling heat flux from infrared measurements
papers.abstract: Recovering a noise-amplified inverse quantity from corrupted boundary data is a recurring problem in physics-informed learning for real-world applications. Specifically, small perturbations in the measured field are magnified through the spatial derivatives needed to reconstruct the target, and hence conventional discretization solvers turn them into large unphysical oscillations. We study this problem through the reconstruction of local time-resolved nucleate-boiling heat flux, which cannot be measured directly and must be inferred from infrared surface temperatures by solving an unsteady three-dimensional heat-conduction problem with sharp and rapidly evolving liquid–vapor interface gradients. We show that neither network architecture nor optimizer alone overcomes the spectral bias that smooths away these interface-scale features, and that the two must be addressed jointly. Our approach combines a Chebyshev physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PIKAN) backbone, a quasi-second-order (SOAP) optimizer, and a temperature-annealed residual-based resampling scheme that concentrates collocation points at high-residual interface regions. Trained directly on experimental infrared measurements imposed as a boundary condition, the network resolves high-frequency bubble signatures and the high-flux distribution tail much better than a Fourier-feature PINN of equal size and training budget. In particular, it selectively filters measurement noise while preserving the physically meaningful high-frequency features, suppressing the spurious oscillations that contaminate finite-volume reconstructions and yielding more physically consistent heat-flux estimates from noisy experimental data.

papers.title: BIM and AI for optimising energy, economy, and environment in construction projects: Systematic review (2014–2026)
papers.abstract: Buildings account for roughly 37% of global energy use and 40% of energy-related CO 2 emissions, yet Building Information Modelling (BIM) and artificial intelligence (AI) are seldom combined to address energy, economy, and environment (the 3E nexus) simultaneously. However, existing reviews have not systematically examined the joint application of BIM and AI to address 3E objectives across the full project lifecycle in a PRISMA 2020-compliant review. This paper synthesises 57 primary studies (2014–2026) from four databases, with within-rater screening agreement κ = 0.83 . Five themes structure the review: BIM–BEM interoperability, AI-driven energy prediction and multi-objective design optimisation, AI-based HVAC control, lifecycle carbon assessment, and digital twins for 3E co-optimisation. Most strikingly, only 5 of 57 studies (9%) address energy, cost, and carbon in a single workflow. Four gaps, namely fragmented IFC/gbXML toolchains, single-dimension optimisation, limited representation of Global South contexts, and the lack of an end-to-end digital twin pipeline, motivate seven prioritised research directions with stakeholder mapping and feasibility assessments.

papers.title: Spend the Budget on the Known or the Unknown? Open-Set Active Learning Scores Two Opposed Objectives Under One Name, Its Filtering Side's Own Results Do Not Treat Unknowns as Waste, and the Winner Is Set by a Relevance Label and a Query Price the Benchmarks Fix in Advance
papers.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Active learning chooses which unlabelled examples a human should label. When the unlabelled pool contains classes the model has never been shown, two lines of work give opposite instructions under the same name. One, usually called open-set active learning or active open-set annotation, counts every queried example from an unseen class as spent budget and builds detectors to keep such examples out of the query. The other, filed under open-world active learning or active category discovery, treats those same examples as the reason to query at all, and rewards a method for finding new classes quickly. This paper reads both literatures against each other. It confirms the premise that their scores are not interchangeable: the published cross-evaluations located, all three run from the discovery side, find the filtering methods mostly losing on discovery measures, though one reports a mixed picture for two of them, and the one that splits old from new classes finds them behind on new classes in every case and mixed on the old: within about 4 points, and ahead in two of six cases. It then complicates the premise. The filtering side's own ablations and settings contradict its framing: leading methods deliberately aim for about 40 percent unknowns per query, report that accuracy barely moves when that target varies, lose sharply when the queried unknowns are removed from detector training, and cluster the unknowns they claim to discard. What separates the two camps is therefore not whether an unknown is worth a query. It is two quantities fixed by the benchmark rather than the data: which held-out classes count as irrelevant, and what an annotator's answer about an unknown costs. The same kind of held-out class is noise in one protocol and a discovery target in the next, and one published sweep shows purity-first methods pulling clearly ahead of informativeness-first ones as the assumed price of an unknown rises, from differences of under a point at the lowest price. The paper proposes a reporting standard under which the two objectives could at least be compared.

papers.title: Unified analytical thermal modeling of laser powder bed fusion: Integration of semi-infinite heat conduction and boundary effects
papers.abstract: This article proposes a novel implementation of a classic analytical thermal model for a moving heat source in bounded regions, building on the exact solution for the temperature distribution arising from a stationary heat source in a wedge with zero-flux boundaries. With the implementation of this boundary-aware basis, the model, for the first time, provides a single closed-form solution that accounts for both conduction in a semi-infinite domain and boundary effects simultaneously, eliminating the need for separate calculations for each. Furthermore, the primary significance of the proposed model lies in its applicability to various elementary boundary types, including convex and concave corners, straight sides, and curved boundaries when the latter are supplied to the model as linear-segment discretization. Moreover, another strength of this model is its ability to predict boundary effects on the melt pool in arbitrary convex polygon geometry by treating each polygon as a combination of straight sides and corners and implementing the superposition of their corresponding simple solutions. Initially, the model is evaluated in distinct corners with different angles by moving the laser parallel to the sides at different offsets. Subsequently, to investigate the impacts of scan path, various scan strategies are applied to square, triangular and hexagonal geometries. Melt pool depth, as an indicator of the accuracy of the predicted temperature distribution, is used for model validation by comparing the results obtained from the proposed model with those from numerical simulation, demonstrating good agreement. The results reveal that as the boundary angle becomes sharper and the laser moves closer to the boundaries, greater heat accumulation and deeper melt pools are observed. The generality and applicability of this analytical model to arbitrary part geometry and scan paths make it a beneficial tool for detecting heat accumulation and evaluation of scan paths.

papers.title: Nurturing an Understanding of Trustworthiness in Cross-Cultural Doctoral Research: An Autoethnography Exploring Active Learning in Higher Education
papers.abstract: University leaders, researchers, students, and policymakers frequently call for increased active learning in higher education. Within this context, novice scholars grapple with how to meaningfully nurture an understanding of trustworthiness throughout the doctoral research process. This study addresses that gap by examining how an innovative reflexive binning system, grounded in the ICAP framework and informed by multilayered reflexivity, can help novice scholars develop an understanding of trustworthiness in cross-cultural doctoral research. Using autoethnography combined with visual vignettes, the study traces the author’s development as a doctoral student learning to engage with qualitative inquiry in reflexive and relational ways. The study examines how developing a reflexive binning system served as a methodological tool for building an understanding of trustworthiness and how engagement with the system reflected progression across the modes of the ICAP framework. The reflexive bins system organizes data across literature, artifacts, experiences, and interviews while integrating structured generative questions and interactive dialogue. Multilayered reflexivity provides the analytic lens for examining how self, interpersonal, and collective dimensions of reflexivity shaped meaning-making across the research process. Two visual vignettes demonstrate how the system functions in practice, making visible the processes through which meaning is constructed, challenged, and refined. The manuscript suggests that reflexive bins foster a deeper understanding of trustworthiness by embedding active learning, reflexive engagement, and relational accountability throughout the research process. This study offers guidance to higher education professionals seeking to support doctoral students in strengthening their understanding of trustworthiness as they transition to independent scholars.

papers.title: SYNTHOS A Research Digital Twin for Oncology: Architecture, Prognostic Engine, Verification and a Programme for Its Validation
papers.abstract: Background. Prognosis in oncology is communicated mostly through population survival curves, which describe groups and say little about the person asking. Computational “digital twins” promise individual projection, but they are often presented with a precision that their inputs and validation cannot support. Aim. This thesis describes and examines SYNTHOS, a research digital twin for oncology built by the author Dr. Dimitrio G. Kimoglou as a single browser application with an optional statistical workbench (NEXUS). It sets out the design, documents what each component computes, tests its numerical routines, states its limits, and designs a programme by which its claims could be refuted. Approach. The software draws its knowledge from a seventy-eight-chapter treatise (263 entities in thirteen groups) and combines a heuristic prognostic index, confidence-based shrinkage, Monte Carlo propagation of uncertainty, a four-lens comparison with an explicit discordance measure, a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis, additive what-if scenarios, a cohort analyser, and a workbench of survival, meta-analytic, simulation and calculator routines. The thesis reads the code, reconstructs the formulae, re-computes the survival and meta-analytic kernels against SciPy and statsmodels, and records where the code and the descriptive text disagree. Screenshots of a demonstration case are included throughout. Findings. The statistical kernels of NEXUS reproduce independent computations to numerical precision in the cases tested. The prognostic index, in contrast, is a heuristic whose weights are not fitted to outcome data, and the thesis says so. The review of the code also found several defects and design limits, among them a cohort analyser that fails to pair some survival columns, a modifier whose effective range is narrower than its nominal range, a molecular lens centred on breast cancer, local storage of identifiers, and external font requests that mean the program is not strictly offline. These are disclosed and are not hidden. Limitations. No outcome validation has been done. The index must not be read as a probability. The software is not a medical device. Conclusion. The contribution is a transparent, inspectable and honestly bounded research instrument, together with a validation programme and pre-stated criteria for failure. Whether it deserves any clinical role is a question that only prospective, independent evaluation can answer. Keywords: digital twin; oncology; prognosis; uncertainty quantification; survival analysis; Monte Carlo; software verification; research ethics; medical device regulation

papers.title: Enhancing Specific Stiffness of Nano‐Architected Materials Through Generative AI and Active Learning
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Architected materials derive their high performance from geometry as much as from intrinsic material properties, yet most optimization frameworks search within predefined topology families, limiting the discovery of genuinely new morphologies. Here, we investigate whether superior architectures exist beyond the reach of these parameterized families, and demonstrate that they can be systematically discovered. We present a framework that searches directly in voxelated structural space. Cubic‐symmetric unit cells drawn from strut‐based, TPMS‐based, and hybrid families are encoded into a continuous latent representation, and surrogate‐guided multi‐objective search with an active learning loop repeatedly converts promising predictions into high‐fidelity validated data. Across nine rounds, the mean minimum Hamming distance from the initial dataset increases from 442 to 641 and the Pareto hypervolume rises from 0.106 to 0.113, confirming systematic expansion of the validated design domain. Computationally, the discovered architectures achieve 11–20% higher relative Young's modulus than initial designs at matched density. Fabricated via two‐photon polymerization and pyrolysis, the optimized carbon nano‐architectures outperform density‐matched counterparts by 18–23% in Young's modulus and 26–40% in strength, reaching specific stiffnesses of 17.2, 22.3, and 21.3 MPa m 3 kg − 1 . These results establish that direct learning in structural space enables discovering mechanically efficient nano‐architectures beyond the initial parameterized families.
